subject: Climate & Environment
title: Smog in Modern Megacities
description: Learn Smog in Modern Megacities in one minute.

hook.text: Delhi, Beijing, and Lahore regularly hit PM2.5 levels 20 times above WHO safety limits.

buildup.text: Rapid industrialization, coal power, and millions of vehicles crowd the air with pollutants.

discovery.text: Crop burning in surrounding farmland adds massive seasonal spikes to city pollution.

twist.text: Schools close, flights cancel, and hospitals fill during the worst smog events.

climax.text: China cut PM2.5 by 40% in major cities between 2013 and 2020 through aggressive regulation.

punchline.text: Megacity smog is a crisis — and China proved it can be fought.

quiz.question: How much did China reduce PM2.5 in major cities between 2013 and 2020?

details.summary: Megacities like Delhi, Beijing, and Lagos suffer severe smog episodes where PM2.5 levels reach ten or more times WHO guidelines. Rapid urbanization, vehicle growth, industrial emissions, and weather patterns combine to create persistent pollution crises.
details.whyItMatters: Over a billion people live in megacities with chronically hazardous air. These cities test whether economic growth can be decoupled from pollution.
takeaways: Delhi routinely records PM2.5 above 300 micrograms per cubic meter
Temperature inversions trap pollution near the ground for days
China's aggressive policies cut PM2.5 in Beijing by roughly 40 percent in a decade

faq.question: Why does Delhi's air quality crash every winter?
faq.answer: Crop-residue burning in neighboring states coincides with cooler temperatures that create temperature inversions, trapping pollutants near the surface. Diwali fireworks and construction dust add to the toxic mix each November.

faq.question: How did Beijing reduce its PM2.5 levels so quickly?
faq.answer: China closed or relocated heavy industries, replaced coal heating with gas, restricted vehicle numbers, and imposed strict emission standards. PM2.5 in Beijing dropped roughly 40 percent between 2013 and 2023.
